P2Q58.q: According to Aquinas, what is the basic principle that divides every human virtue into either an intellectual or a moral virtue?
options: Whether the virtue was acquired by habituation or given by nature
Whether the virtue perfects the reason/intellect or perfects the appetite
Whether the virtue concerns God or concerns created things
Whether the virtue is found in children or only in adults
P2Q58.explanation: Aquinas holds there are only two principles of human action, reason and appetite; a virtue perfecting reason is intellectual, one perfecting appetite is moral.

P2Q58.q: Why does Aquinas reject Socrates's view that 'every virtue is a kind of prudence' and that all who sin do so through ignorance?
options: Because Socrates denied that virtue can be taught
Because it wrongly reduces all virtue to a perfection of reason alone, ignoring the appetite's need for its own perfecting habits
Because Socrates confused virtue with pleasure
Because prudence, for Aquinas, is not really a virtue at all
P2Q58.explanation: Aquinas presents Socrates's opinion that reason alone governs human acts (like a despot ruling a body with no power to resist), which would make all virtue intellectual; Aquinas instead holds the appetite has its own principles requiring moral virtue.

P2Q58.q: Which intellectual virtues, according to Article 4, can moral virtue NOT exist without?
options: Wisdom and science
Art and science
Understanding and prudence
Speculative wisdom alone
P2Q58.explanation: Aquinas states moral virtue can lack wisdom, science, and art, but cannot exist without understanding (of first principles) and prudence (right reason about action).

P2Q59.q: Which of the following is one of Aquinas's three reasons that moral virtue itself cannot be a passion?
options: Passions are always evil, while virtue is always good
A passion is a movement of the sensitive appetite, whereas virtue is a habit, a principle of that movement, not the movement itself
Passions belong only to animals, not to rational beings
Virtue can only be found in the intellect, never in the appetite
P2Q59.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons: passion is a movement while virtue is a stable habit; passions are not in themselves good or evil while virtue is referable to good alone; and the movement of passion runs from appetite to reason while virtue's movement runs from reason to appetite.

P2Q59.q: In the dispute Aquinas reports between the Stoics and the Peripatetics (followers of Aristotle) on virtue and passion, what was the Peripatetic position that Aquinas favors?
options: That passions must be entirely eliminated for virtue to exist
That passions are compatible with moral virtue when they are reduced to the rational mean
That only negative passions like fear are compatible with virtue
That passions are irrelevant to virtue altogether
P2Q59.explanation: Aquinas notes the Stoics held the wise man has no passions, while the Peripatetics (Aristotle's school) held passions are compatible with virtue provided they are moderated to the mean; Aquinas sides with the Peripatetic view.

P2Q59.q: Why, according to Article 5, can moral virtue not exist entirely without passion (understood as movements of the sensitive appetite)?
options: Because reason cannot function without emotional stimulation
Because virtue would otherwise leave the sensitive appetite idle instead of directing it to its proper regulated activity
Because Scripture requires that virtuous people feel strong emotions
Because passions are identical to virtuous acts
P2Q59.explanation: Aquinas argues it is not virtue's function to make the appetitive powers idle, but to direct them to their proper acts under reason's command, just as virtue directs the bodily limbs rather than immobilizing them.

P2Q60.q: According to Article 3, what single formal notion do all the moral virtues concerned with external operations (such as religion, piety, and gratitude) share?
options: The notion of pleasure moderated by reason
The notion of justice, i.e., rendering something due to another
The notion of courage in the face of danger
The notion of custom passed down by ancestors
P2Q60.explanation: Aquinas explains that virtues about operations bear the character of justice because they concern rendering something due to another, though the kind of debt differs (to God in religion, to parents/country in piety, to benefactors in gratitude).

P2Q60.q: Why, per Article 5, can several distinct moral virtues share one and the same passion as their common object (e.g., several virtues concerned with pleasure)?
options: Because virtues are differentiated by their relation to reason, while passions are differentiated by their relation to the sensitive appetite, so the two do not have to divide the same way
Because Aquinas denies that virtues have distinct objects at all
Because all passions are ultimately reducible to fear
Because pleasure is not really a passion
P2Q60.explanation: Aquinas argues that since virtue's perfection depends on reason while passion's nature depends on the sensitive appetite, one object can generate diverse passions without diverse virtues, or diverse virtues without diverse passions.

P2Q60.q: What determines, according to Article 1, that the moral virtues are specifically different from one another rather than being a single virtue?
options: The differing intensity with which people practice them
Habits differ specifically according to the specific differences of their objects
The differing ages at which people acquire them
Whether the virtue is praised by many people or few
P2Q60.explanation: Aquinas's principle is that habits differ specifically according to the specific differences of their objects; since moral virtues concern really different objects of appetite, they are specifically distinct habits, not one virtue.

P2Q61.q: Why does Aquinas call the moral virtues (together with prudence) the 'cardinal' or 'principal' virtues?
options: Because they were the first virtues named in Scripture
Because, unlike merely intellectual virtues without moral virtue, they involve rectitude of the appetite and so actually cause good deeds to be done, not merely confer the ability to do them
Because Aristotle numbered exactly four of them
Because they are easier to acquire than other virtues
P2Q61.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes perfect virtue, which requires rectitude of the appetite and actually causes the good deed, from imperfect virtue, which only confers the ability; the perfect kind (moral virtues and prudence) are therefore called principal or cardinal.

P2Q61.q: According to Article 3, in which kind of matter is the virtue of fortitude's characteristic good chiefly found?
options: In matters of food and drink
In distributions and exchanges between persons
In perils of death, which are hardest to withstand
In the private counsel of reason
P2Q61.explanation: Aquinas identifies the good of firmness in holding to reason against the impulse of passion as found chiefly in perils of death, which is why fortitude concerns that matter above all.

P2Q61.q: In Article 5's account of the 'exemplar' virtues pre-existing in God, what does temperance correspond to in God?
options: God's unchangeableness
The turning of God's gaze upon Himself, just as temperance conforms the human appetite to reason
God's observance of the Eternal Law in His works
God's power to create out of nothing
P2Q61.explanation: Aquinas, following Plotinus/Macrobius, says that just as temperance in us conforms appetite to reason, in God temperance is figured as God's gaze turned wholly upon Himself, while fortitude corresponds to His unchangeableness and justice to His observance of the Eternal Law.

P2Q62.q: Why does Aquinas say man needs virtues beyond the naturally acquirable moral and intellectual virtues?
options: Because natural virtues are always counterfeit
Because a happiness surpassing human nature, attainable only by God's power, requires additional principles that direct man toward that supernatural end
Because moral virtues are incompatible with each other
Because only priests need additional virtues
P2Q62.explanation: Aquinas argues that besides the natural happiness proportionate to human nature, there is a supernatural happiness obtainable only by God's power; theological virtues are the additional principles God infuses to direct man toward it.

P2Q62.q: According to Article 2, why are the theological virtues specifically distinct from the intellectual and moral virtues?
options: Because they cannot be lost once possessed
Because their object is God Himself, surpassing the grasp of human reason, whereas the object of intellectual and moral virtue is something reason can comprehend
Because they are only found in clergy
Because they involve no habits at all
P2Q62.explanation: Habits are specifically distinguished by the formal difference of their objects; since the theological virtues' object is God as He surpasses reason's grasp, while moral and intellectual virtues have objects comprehensible to reason, they differ in species.

P2Q62.q: In Article 4, why does faith precede hope, and hope precede charity, in the order of generation?
options: Because faith is easier to obtain than the other two
Because the appetite cannot tend toward (hope for or love) something unless it is first apprehended, and it is faith that lets the intellect apprehend the object of hope and love
Because Scripture lists them in that order arbitrarily
Because charity is a purely intellectual virtue
P2Q62.explanation: Aquinas reasons that the movement of the appetite toward hoping or loving something requires that thing first be apprehended by intellect; faith supplies that apprehension, so it precedes hope, and hoping in someone in turn disposes one to love him.

P2Q63.q: What does Aquinas conclude in Article 2 about how acquired virtue is caused in us by habituation?
options: Acquired virtue arises purely by chance with no natural basis
Man's good is measured against a rule (human reason or Divine Law), and repeated good acts under that rule produce the corresponding habit of virtue
Habituation can never actually produce real virtue
All acquired virtues come from imitating angels
P2Q63.explanation: Aquinas explains that virtue perfects man in relation to good, which must be measured by a rule (reason, or the higher Divine Law), and that virtues are produced from acts performed in accordance with that rule, as discussed regarding habits generally.

P2Q63.q: Why, according to Article 3, must some moral virtues be directly infused by God rather than acquired?
options: Because acquired virtues are evil
Because effects must be proportionate to their causes, and virtues directing us to a supernatural end require principles beyond the natural ones from which acquired virtues arise
Because infused virtues are easier to obtain than acquired ones
Because Aristotle taught that all virtue must be infused
P2Q63.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as God bestows the theological virtues to direct us to a supernatural end beyond natural principles, He must also infuse corresponding moral virtues proportionate to that supernatural end, since acquired virtue alone arises only from natural principles.

P2Q63.q: Why does Aquinas conclude in Article 4 that infused temperance and acquired temperance are actually different in species, despite sharing a name?
options: Because infused temperance concerns different bodily organs

Because the two are measured by different rules -- human reason sets one mean (e.g., not harming health) while the Divine rule sets another (e.g., chastising the body) -- and the object's formal aspect comes from its rule
Because acquired temperance is only found in pagans
Because infused temperance produces no real self-control
P2Q63.explanation: Aquinas holds that a virtue's formal object comes from the rule that fixes its mean; since the mean of concupiscence fixed by human reason differs from that fixed by the Divine rule (e.g., 1 Corinthians 9:27 on chastising the body), infused and acquired temperance differ in species.

P2Q64.q: According to Article 1, why does moral virtue observe a mean between excess and deficiency?
options: Because all human actions are naturally moderate

Because the good of anything ruled or measured consists in conformity to its rule, and reason is the measure of the appetite's movement, so virtue's good lies between excess and deficient conformity to reason
Because the passions are naturally balanced
Because Aristotle commanded it by definition alone, with no underlying reason
P2Q64.explanation: Aquinas argues moral virtue perfects the appetite, whose rule and measure is reason; since the good of a measured thing lies in conforming to its measure, and departure from that conformity happens by excess or deficiency, virtue's good is a mean.

P2Q64.q: In Article 2, is the mean of moral virtue a mean in the thing itself (a 'real' mean) or a mean set by reason in relation to us?
options: It is the mean fixed by reason in the particular matter, since moral virtue perfects the act of the appetite according to reason's ordering, not the act of reason itself
It is a purely mathematical mean identical for every person
It is whatever the majority of people in a society consider acceptable
It is a mean fixed only by physical necessity, unrelated to reason
P2Q64.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the mean as it might apply to reason's own act from the mean that reason establishes in some matter for us; moral virtue's mean is of the second kind, a rational mean set in the appetite's matter.

P2Q64.q: According to Article 4, why do the theological virtues NOT observe a mean the way moral virtues do?
options: Because they are not really virtues in the strict sense
Because their measure is God Himself, whose goodness, truth, and power we can never equal or exceed, so there is no possibility of excess, only greater or lesser approach to the summit
Because theological virtues are entirely a matter of feeling, not reason
Because they only apply to acts, never to habits
P2Q64.explanation: Aquinas explains that since God is the very rule of the theological virtues, and we can never love, believe, or hope in Him more than He deserves, there is no possible excess -- the good of these virtues instead increases the closer it approaches that unlimited summit.

P2Q65.q: According to Article 1, why are the moral virtues NOT necessarily connected with one another when considered as imperfect (mere natural or habituated inclinations)?
options: Because a person could, by temperament or habituation, be prompt to acts of one virtue (e.g., liberality) without being prompt to acts of another (e.g., chastity)
Because imperfect virtues are always false virtues and do not really exist
Because Aristotle denied that any virtues could be connected
Because imperfect virtues can only exist in animals
P2Q65.explanation: Aquinas notes that as mere inclinations, whether natural or from habituation, moral virtues need not accompany one another -- someone can be inclined to liberality without being inclined to chastity -- so connection applies properly only to perfect virtue.

P2Q65.q: Why, according to Article 2, can genuine perfect moral virtue never exist without charity?
options: Because charity is required for prudence to be well-disposed toward the last end, and prudence is required by all the other moral virtues
Because charity makes a person emotionally happy, which is required for any virtue
Because pagans could never possess any virtue at all
Because charity replaces the need for prudence entirely
P2Q65.explanation: Aquinas argues that prudence requires being well disposed toward the ultimate end, which is the effect of charity, even more than being disposed toward other, lesser ends; since the moral virtues cannot exist without prudence, and infused prudence cannot exist without charity, neither can perfect moral virtue.

P2Q65.q: What analogy does Aquinas use in Article 3 to explain why all the moral virtues are infused together with charity?
options: An analogy to a king granting titles to subjects

An analogy to nature, where whatever contains a principle of certain works is also given the organs necessary to carry them out, just as charity as principle of good works toward the last end comes with the moral virtues needed to perform them
An analogy to seeds growing into trees over many years
An analogy between charity and physical strength
P2Q65.explanation: Aquinas reasons that God works no less perfectly in grace than in nature, and in nature whatever has a principle of activity is equipped with what is needed to carry it out (like an animal's organs); so charity, as principle of good works toward man's last end, comes with the moral virtues needed for those works.

P2Q66.q: According to Article 1, why does prudence surpass the other moral virtues in goodness among virtues of different species?
options: Because prudence is easier to acquire
Because the cause is more excellent than its effect, and prudence perfects reason itself, the root of human good, which the other moral virtues only partake of
Because prudence was mentioned first by Aristotle
Because prudence alone can be practiced without effort
P2Q66.explanation: Aquinas argues that reason is the cause and root of human good, so prudence, which perfects reason directly, surpasses the other moral virtues, which perfect the appetite only insofar as it shares in reason -- with justice (in the will) ranking above fortitude, and fortitude above temperance.

P2Q66.q: According to Article 3, why are the intellectual virtues, speaking simply (absolutely), more excellent than the moral virtues?
options: Because intellectual virtues are always more useful in daily life
Because the object of reason (the universal) is more excellent than the object of appetite (particular things), even though moral virtue can be more necessary relatively speaking for someone in need
Because moral virtues are not really virtues but only habits
Because the Church ranks intellectual virtues higher in official teaching
P2Q66.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes 'simply' from 'relatively': a virtue is more excellent simply according to the excellence of its object, and reason's object (the universal) outranks the appetite's object (the particular), so intellectual virtues are simply more excellent, even where moral virtue may be relatively more needed.

P2Q66.q: Why, according to Article 4, does Aquinas rank justice as the most excellent of the moral virtues?
options: Because justice is the oldest virtue historically
Because its subject is the will (the rational appetite) and its object concerns ordering man rightly not only in himself but toward another person
Because justice requires the least self-control of any virtue
Because justice is easier to legislate than other virtues
P2Q66.explanation: Aquinas explains justice is most excellent because, as to subject, it resides in the will, the rational appetite, and as to object/matter, it concerns operations ordering man toward others, not himself alone -- making it 'the most excellent of virtues' as Aristotle says.

P2Q67.q: According to Article 6, what happens to charity after this life, in the state of glory?
options: Charity disappears entirely, replaced by faith
Charity remains identically the same, since love's nature does not include imperfection and can relate either to a possessed or an unpossessed object
Charity is transformed into a completely different virtue with a new name
Charity is reduced to a lesser form of hope
P2Q67.explanation: Aquinas argues that unlike faith and hope, whose very natures imply an imperfection (something unseen or unpossessed) that is removed in glory, charity's nature as love does not include imperfection, so it passes into glory identically the same.

P2Q67.q: Why, according to Article 4, does hope not remain after death in the state of glory?
options: Because hope was never a true theological virtue to begin with
Because hope denotes a movement toward a good not yet possessed, and movement of its nature ceases once that good is actually possessed (the enjoyment of God)
Because hope is replaced immediately by fear in the afterlife
Because only faith and charity were ever counted as theological virtues
P2Q67.explanation: Aquinas reasons that whatever implies imperfection of its subject by its very nature (like movement, which is 'the act of that which is in potentiality') cannot coexist with the opposite perfection; since hope is a movement toward unpossessed good, it ceases once God is actually possessed and enjoyed.

P2Q67.q: According to Article 3, why does faith not remain, as faith, after this life?
options: Because faith was only ever a metaphor, not a real virtue
Because faith and the beatific vision stand as imperfect knowledge versus perfect knowledge, and opposition between perfection and imperfection means both cannot be in the same subject at once
Because faith is replaced by hope in glory
Because faith only applies to non-believers
P2Q67.explanation: Aquinas argues that perfection and imperfection are opposed as contraries admitting of more and less, so they cannot coexist in the same subject; since faith is an imperfect kind of knowledge, it is excluded once the perfect knowledge of the beatific vision is attained, though it remains generically as a kind of knowledge.

P2Q68.q: According to Article 3, how are the gifts of the Holy Ghost related to the Holy Ghost, by analogy with the moral virtues?
options: The gifts are unrelated to any power the way virtues relate to reason
Just as moral virtues dispose the appetitive powers to obey reason promptly, the gifts are habits disposing man to obey readily the promptings of the Holy Ghost
The gifts replace the need for the Holy Ghost's assistance entirely
The gifts are identical in every respect to the moral virtues
P2Q68.explanation: Aquinas draws a direct analogy: as moral virtues are habits perfecting the appetite so it obeys reason's command promptly, the gifts of the Holy Ghost are habits perfecting man so he readily follows the Holy Ghost's promptings.

P2Q68.q: According to Article 5, what virtue unites all the gifts of the Holy Ghost together, so that whoever has it has all the gifts?
options: Prudence
Faith
Charity, since the Holy Ghost dwells in us by charity
Fortitude
P2Q68.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as the moral virtues are united in prudence, the gifts of the Holy Ghost are connected together in charity, because the Holy Ghost dwells in us through charity (Romans 5:5).

P2Q68.q: According to Article 2, why are the gifts of the Holy Ghost necessary for man's salvation?
options: Because human reason alone is always sufficient for every good act
Because in matters where the prompting of reason is not sufficient, man needs the prompting of the Holy Ghost, for which the gifts dispose him
Because the gifts replace baptism as the means of salvation
Because Scripture requires exactly seven virtues to be listed
P2Q68.explanation: Aquinas explains that the gifts are perfections disposing man to be amenable to God's promptings; since reason's own prompting is not always sufficient, there is a need, in such matters, for the further prompting of the Holy Ghost through the gifts.

P2Q69.q: According to Article 1, how do the beatitudes differ from the virtues and the gifts?
options: They differ as a lower power differs from a higher power
They differ as act differs from habit -- the beatitudes are the acts/works flowing from virtues and especially from the gifts
They do not differ at all; the terms are simply synonyms
They differ because beatitudes belong only to angels, not to men
P2Q69.explanation: Aquinas argues that we approach and are moved toward the happy end through the works of virtue, and especially the gifts; the beatitudes therefore differ from the virtues and gifts not as one habit differs from another, but as act differs from habit.

P2Q69.q: According to Article 3, how does contemplative happiness relate to the future beatitude for which the beatitudes give hope?
options: It is entirely unrelated to future beatitude
It is an obstacle to future beatitude, just like sensual happiness
If perfect, it is the very essence of future beatitude, and if imperfect, it is a beginning of it
It is only relevant to angels, not to human beings
P2Q69.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes three kinds of happiness people have proposed -- sensual, active, and contemplative -- and states that sensual happiness obstructs future beatitude, active happiness disposes toward it, while contemplative happiness, if perfect, constitutes its very essence, and if imperfect, is its beginning.

P2Q69.q: According to Article 4, why does Our Lord promise 'the kingdom of heaven' as the reward to the poor in spirit specifically among the first beatitudes?
options: Because poverty is inherently more virtuous than any other condition
Because men who seek excellence and abundance wrongly in external riches and honors are shown that true excellence and abundance are instead found in God's kingdom
Because the poor in spirit have no need of any reward at all
Because the phrase is purely symbolic and has no connection to worldly ambition
P2Q69.explanation: Aquinas explains that the rewards of the first three beatitudes correspond to what men wrongly seek in earthly happiness; since men seek excellence and abundance in riches and honors, the kingdom of heaven -- true excellence and abundance in God -- is promised to the poor in spirit instead.

P2Q70.q: According to Article 1, in the sense in which 'fruit' applies to man's spiritual life, what does 'fruit' properly mean?
options: Any virtuous habit a person possesses
That which is last and gives pleasure -- man's last end, intended for his own enjoyment
Every single action a person performs, virtuous or not
The physical rewards a person receives for good behavior
P2Q70.explanation: Aquinas explains that just as fruit among material things is the last, sweet product of a plant, so spiritually a man's 'fruit' is that ultimate and delightful thing -- his last end -- which he intends for his enjoyment, not everything he produces or gathers.

P2Q70.q: According to Article 2, how do the fruits of the Holy Ghost differ from the beatitudes?
options: The fruits require more perfection than the beatitudes do
A fruit need only be something ultimate and delightful, while a beatitude must be something perfect and excellent, so all beatitudes are fruits but not all fruits are beatitudes
The fruits belong to the intellect while the beatitudes belong only to the will
There is no real difference; Aquinas treats the terms as fully interchangeable
P2Q70.explanation: Aquinas states that a fruit need only be ultimate and delightful, any virtuous deed one delights in, whereas a beatitude requires perfection and excellence and pertains specifically to the gifts; hence all beatitudes are fruits, but not every fruit rises to a beatitude.

P2Q70.q: According to Article 4, why are the fruits of the Spirit contrary, in general, to the works of the flesh?
options: Because they concern completely unrelated subject matters

Because the Holy Ghost moves the mind toward what is in accord with, or above, reason, while the fleshly appetite draws man down toward sensible goods beneath him, making the two like contrary (upward vs. downward) movements
Because the works of the flesh are not really sins in Aquinas's view
Because the fruits of the Spirit apply only to celibate persons
P2Q70.explanation: Aquinas compares the fruits of the Spirit, which move the mind toward what accords with or surpasses reason, to the works of the flesh, which draw man toward goods beneath him, likening the opposition to the contrary physical movements of upward and downward.

P2Q71.q: According to Article 1, what does vice directly imply, on Aquinas's account?
options: A disposition whereby the subject is well disposed according to the mode of its nature -- vice implies the contrary of this
An emotion that a person cannot control under any circumstances
A punishment imposed by civil law
A physical illness of the body
P2Q71.explanation: Aquinas explains virtue directly implies a disposition of a thing being well-disposed according to its nature; vice, being contrary to virtue, therefore implies the corresponding lack of that natural fittingness.

P2Q71.q: According to Article 3, which is worse: the habit of vice itself, or a single vicious act?
options: The habit of vice is always worse than any act proceeding from it
The vicious act is worse than the vicious habit, since in both good and evil, act precedes habit and habit is called good or bad only because of the goodness or badness of the acts it produces
They are always exactly equal in badness
Neither can be compared, since habits and acts belong to entirely different categories
P2Q71.explanation: Aquinas argues that habit stands midway between power and act, and since 'the cause of a thing being such is yet more so,' the act surpasses the habit in goodness or badness -- so a vicious act is worse than the vicious habit that inclines to it.

P2Q71.q: According to Article 4, why can a person possessing a virtue still commit a single act of sin without immediately destroying that virtue as a habit?
options: Because virtues in the soul, unlike natural forms, do not necessarily produce their effect -- man uses a habit only when he wills, so one contrary act does not by itself destroy a habit not engendered by one act
Because sin and virtue are actually the same thing under different names
Because virtues, once acquired, can never be lost under any circumstances
Because Aquinas denies that virtuous people can ever sin
P2Q71.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the soul's habits from natural forms that necessarily produce their proper operation; since a habit is used only when the will chooses, one sinful act does not destroy the virtue as habit, though mortal sin does expel infused virtues 'as virtues' by banishing charity, their root.

P2Q72.q: According to Article 1, what determines the specific difference between one sin and another?
options: The severity of the punishment attached to each sin
The objects of the voluntary acts, since the species of a thing comes from what is essential (the voluntary act intended) rather than from what is accidental (the resulting inordinateness)
The particular emotion felt while committing the sin
The number of people affected by the sin
P2Q72.explanation: Aquinas argues that of the two elements in sin -- the voluntary act and its inordinateness (a departure from God's law) -- the voluntary act is essential while the inordinateness is accidental to the sinner's intention; since species follows from what is essential, sins are distinguished specifically by the objects of their voluntary acts.

P2Q72.q: According to Article 3, why do sins NOT differ specifically according to their moving/efficient causes (such as fear or love prompting the sin)?
options: Because moving causes always determine only one possible outcome, unlike ends

Because, unlike natural active principles which are fixed to one effect, the active principles of voluntary acts (like fear or love) are not determined to any one act, so the same passion can lead to different sins, while species is instead determined by the end/object intended
Because Aquinas holds that human acts have no causes at all
Because emotions are never involved in the commission of sin
P2Q72.explanation: Aquinas notes that natural causes are fixed to produce one determinate effect (heat always causes heating), but voluntary active principles like fear or love are not so determined -- the same fear could lead to theft, murder, or neglect of duty -- so sins are specifically distinguished by their end and object, not by their motive cause.

P2Q72.q: According to Article 4, on what basis does Aquinas divide sin into sin against God, against oneself, and against one's neighbor?
options: On the basis of a threefold order man is subject to: the order of reason, the order of Divine Law (which includes and surpasses reason), and the order relating man to others in society
On the basis of which Commandment is broken numerically
On the basis of the sinner's social class
On the basis of whether the sin is public or private
P2Q72.explanation: Aquinas grounds this threefold division in the orders to which man is subject -- reason, the higher Divine Law (which includes matters surpassing reason, like faith), and the social order toward other men -- corresponding respectively to the theological virtues, temperance/fortitude, and justice.

P2Q73.q: According to Article 2, why does Aquinas reject the Stoic view (as reported via Cicero) that all sins are equal?
options: Because all privations, including sin's departure from reason, are actually simple and admit of no degree

Because sin's privation of due order is not a total, simple privation like death, but one in which something of the order of reason still remains, and such privations admit of more or less depending on what remains
Because the Stoics never actually held this view
Because Aquinas holds that some acts commonly called sins are not really sins at all
P2Q73.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes simple privations (like death or darkness), which admit no degree, from privations like sickness where something of the opposite habit remains; since sin does not destroy the order of reason entirely (or it would destroy itself), it is more like sickness, and sins can therefore differ in gravity.

P2Q73.q: According to Article 3, why is a sin against God (such as blasphemy or unbelief) graver than a sin against external things (such as theft)?
options: Because external things are directed to man as their end, and man himself is directed to God as his end, so the higher the end/object disordered, the graver the sin -- and God is the highest object of all
Because sins against God are punished more severely by human courts
Because theft is not actually considered a sin in Aquinas's system
Because sins against external things are the only sins with an object at all
P2Q73.explanation: Aquinas reasons that gravity follows the object's rank in the order of ends: since external goods are ordered to man and man is ordered to God, a sin directly against the substance of man (murder) is graver than a sin against externals (theft), and a sin directly against God is gravest of all.

P2Q73.q: According to Article 5, which of Aquinas's three reasons explains why spiritual sins are, as such, of greater guilt than carnal sins?
options: Spiritual sin denotes a 'turning away' from God (implicating guilt more directly), while carnal sin is chiefly a disordered 'turning toward' bodily goods
Carnal sins always involve more people than spiritual sins
Spiritual sins are easier to hide from other people
Carnal sins were not considered sins at all by Aquinas
P2Q73.explanation: Among Aquinas's three reasons: spiritual sin more essentially involves turning away from God (the source of guilt), while carnal sin is chiefly a turning toward bodily goods; also spiritual sins offend God and neighbor (owed greater love than one's own body), and carnal sins have the excuse of a stronger innate impulse.

P2Q74.q: According to Article 1, why is the will the proper subject of sin?
options: Because sin, like all moral acts, remains within the agent rather than passing into external matter, and the will is the principle of such voluntary acts
Because sin only ever involves external, physical actions
Because the intellect, not the will, is always the true subject of sin
Because sin cannot be located in any single power of the soul
P2Q74.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes acts that pass into external matter from acts like desiring and knowing that remain in the agent; since moral acts, whether virtuous or sinful, are of the latter kind and are properly voluntary, their principle, the will, is the subject of sin.

P2Q74.q: According to Article 4, why can mortal sin not exist in the sensuality (the sensitive appetite) alone?
options: Because the sensuality is incapable of any movement whatsoever
Because ordering something to the last end belongs to reason alone, not to sensuality, and mortal sin consists precisely in a disorder regarding the last end
Because mortal sin can only be committed by rational angels, not embodied humans
Because sensuality is entirely outside the will's control
P2Q74.explanation: Aquinas argues that mortal sin, being a disorder that destroys the ordering to man's last end, can only occur in the power responsible for ordering things to that end -- reason -- since sensuality has no such function, even though venial-type disorder can occur there.

P2Q74.q: According to Article 8, why is mere delight in the thought of fornication (without consenting to the act) not necessarily a mortal sin?
options: Because thoughts can never be sinful in any way
Because the delight can terminate simply on the thought itself (which is not inherently a mortal sin, sometimes venial, sometimes no sin at all) rather than on the sinful act being consented to
Because only external deeds, never internal thoughts, can be sins
Because fornication itself is not actually a sin according to Aquinas
P2Q74.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes delight terminating in the thought itself (which, depending on purpose, may be no sin, or only venial) from delight terminating in the act thought of (consent to which would be mortal); mere delectation in thinking about a sin, without consenting to the deed, need not be mortal.

P2Q75.q: According to Article 1, how does the will cause both the act of sin and its inordinateness, according to Aquinas?
options: The will causes neither; sin is entirely caused by external demons

The will, lacking the direction of reason and Divine law and intent on some mutable good, causes the act of sin directly, while causing the disorder/inordinateness only indirectly, beside its intention
The inordinateness of sin has no cause whatsoever
God directly causes the inordinateness of every sinful act
P2Q75.explanation: Aquinas argues that the will, when it fails to be ruled by reason and Divine law while pursuing some mutable good, directly causes the sinful act itself, while the resulting disorder follows indirectly and accidentally, since no one intends evil precisely as evil.

P2Q75.q: According to Article 3, why can nothing external be a sufficient cause of sin by itself?
options: Because external things and persons can only move the reason or sensitive appetite, neither of which necessarily determines the will, and only God (who cannot cause sin) can move the will directly
Because external causes have no influence on human action at all
Because sin is entirely random and uncaused
Because only physical objects, never persons, can tempt someone to sin
P2Q75.explanation: Aquinas explains that since only God can move the will directly and He cannot be a cause of sin, external things can only move a person to sin indirectly by influencing reason or the sensitive appetite, neither of which necessitates the will's consent -- so the will alone remains the sufficient, completive cause of sin.

P2Q75.q: According to Article 4, in what way can one sin be the 'material' cause of another, according to Aquinas's example?
options: By directly forcing the will to choose the second sin with no other explanation needed
By preparing the matter for another sin, as when covetousness (hoarding wealth) prepares the matter over which strife later arises
By being completely unrelated to any subsequent sin
By occurring only after the second sin has already been committed
P2Q75.explanation: Aquinas illustrates the material causation of one sin by another with the example of covetousness, which by amassing wealth prepares the very matter (the hoarded goods) that later becomes the occasion for strife.

P2Q76.q: According to Article 1, in what sense can ignorance be a cause of sin?
options: As a direct cause that actively produces the sinful act by its own positive power
As an indirect cause, by removing the impediment (knowledge) that would otherwise have forbidden or prevented the sinful act
Ignorance can never be any kind of cause of sin
Ignorance is identical to the sinful act itself
P2Q76.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes direct causes, which move by their own power, from indirect causes, which remove an impediment; ignorance causes sin in the second way, by being a privation of the knowledge that would have forbidden the sinful act.

P2Q76.q: According to Article 2, which kind of ignorance is a sin, according to Aquinas?
options: All ignorance whatsoever, without exception, counts as sin
Only vincible ignorance (which could be overcome by effort) regarding matters one is bound to know is a sin; invincible ignorance is never a sin
Only ignorance of geometrical theorems is sinful
Ignorance is never sinful under any circumstances
P2Q76.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes vincible ignorance, which can be overcome through effort and is sinful when it concerns what one is obliged to know (such as the articles of faith or one's duties), from invincible ignorance, which cannot be overcome and, being involuntary, is never a sin.

P2Q76.q: According to Article 3, when does ignorance excuse a person from sin altogether?
options: Whenever ignorance of any kind is present in a person, regardless of its relation to the act
Only when the ignorance actually causes the act, making it altogether involuntary -- ignorance that merely accompanies or follows an already-willed act does not excuse
Ignorance can never excuse a person from sin under any circumstances
Only when the ignorant person is a member of the clergy
P2Q76.explanation: Aquinas holds that ignorance excuses from sin only when it is the actual cause of the act (such that knowledge would have prevented it, rendering the act involuntary); ignorance that merely accompanies an act the will was already inclined to perform does not excuse.

P2Q77.q: According to Article 4, what does Aquinas identify as the source of every sin?
options: Ignorance of the natural law
Inordinate love of self, since desiring a temporal good inordinately stems from loving oneself inordinately
A weakness inherited only from Adam's original sin
External temptation from demons, considered apart from the will
P2Q77.explanation: Aquinas reasons that every sinful act proceeds from inordinate desire for some temporal good, and desiring a good inordinately for oneself is itself a mark of loving oneself inordinately; hence inordinate self-love is the cause of every sin.

P2Q77.q: According to Article 3, why does Aquinas call a sin committed through passion a 'sin of weakness,' comparing the sinner to an epileptic?
options: Because passion has no real effect on moral action at all

Because when the concupiscible or irascible power is disturbed by a passion contrary to reason's order, it hinders the soul's due action just as bodily disorder hinders a diseased organ's proper function, as an epileptic's limbs move against his intention
Because weak-willed people are physically ill by definition
Because the term 'weakness' refers only to a lack of physical strength
P2Q77.explanation: Aquinas compares weakness of soul to weakness of body: just as a bodily part fails to perform its healthy function when disordered, the concupiscible or irascible power, when disturbed by passion contrary to reason, impedes due action, much as an epileptic's limbs move contrary to his intention.

P2Q77.q: According to Article 8, can a sin committed through passion be a mortal sin?
options: No, sins committed through passion are always merely venial

Yes -- since proceeding from passion to a sinful act or deliberate consent is not sudden, the deliberating reason has the opportunity to check the passion, and if it fails to do so, the sin can be mortal
No, because passion always removes voluntariness entirely
Yes, but only if the passion was provoked deliberately beforehand, never otherwise
P2Q77.explanation: Aquinas argues that mortal sin requires deliberate turning away from the last end; since movement from passion to sinful consent is not instantaneous, deliberating reason typically has the chance to resist the passion, so failing to do so, as in many murders and adulteries committed through passion, still constitutes mortal sin.

P2Q78.q: According to Article 1, what does it mean to sin 'through certain malice,' or on purpose?
options: To sin accidentally, without any awareness of wrongdoing
To knowingly choose a spiritual evil (loss of a spiritual good) in order to obtain a temporal good the will loves more than the order of reason or Divine law
To sin only when compelled by overwhelming external force
To commit any sin whatsoever, regardless of the sinner's awareness
P2Q78.explanation: Aquinas explains that when the will loves a temporal good more than the order of reason, Divine law, or charity, it knowingly accepts the loss of a spiritual good to obtain that temporal good -- and choosing evil knowingly in this way is sinning through certain malice.

P2Q78.q: According to Article 4, which of Aquinas's three reasons explains why a sin committed through malice is graver than one committed through passion?
options: A sin through malice belongs more to the will itself (which moves to evil of its own accord), while passion-driven sin is impelled by something extrinsic, so, other things equal, the sin is graver the more it stems from the will
Sins through malice are always public while sins through passion are always private
Passion-driven sins involve more people than malice-driven sins
There is no real difference in gravity between the two
P2Q78.explanation: Among Aquinas's three reasons: sin belongs chiefly to an act of will, so a sin through malice (will moved to evil on its own) is graver than one through passion (will moved by something extrinsic); also malice-driven habits persist while passions pass, and malice corrupts the very end pursued.

P2Q78.q: According to Article 3, in what two ways can the will be moved to evil 'of its own accord,' constituting sin through certain malice?
options: Only through direct demonic possession, with no other possibility

Through a corrupt disposition (an acquired vicious habit or a bodily condition) making evil seem suitable, or through the removal of an obstacle such as hope or fear that had been restraining the person from sin
Only through ignorance of the moral law
Only through a single momentary passion that quickly passes
P2Q78.explanation: Aquinas identifies two ways the will tends to evil of its own accord: through a corrupt disposition (habit or bodily condition) making evil seem connaturally suitable, or through the removal of a restraining obstacle, as when hope gives way to despair or fear to presumption.

P2Q79.q: According to Article 1, why can God not be, even indirectly, the cause of sin?
options: Because God does not exist, according to Aquinas, in this context

Because every sin is a departure from the order to God as last end, and God, who turns all things toward Himself as their end, cannot cause a departure from that very order, either in Himself or through withholding assistance unjustly
Because sin is not actually a real thing at all, so it needs no cause
Because only angels, not God, have power over the human will
P2Q79.explanation: Aquinas argues sin is essentially a departure from the order that leads to God as last end; since God draws all things toward Himself, He cannot be the cause of a turning away from that order, and even His withholding of assistance follows the just order of His wisdom, not culpable negligence.

P2Q79.q: According to Article 2, in what sense is the act of sin from God, while the sin itself is not?
options: The act of sin is not from God in any sense whatsoever

As a being and an act, the sinful act is from God (the First Cause of all being and action), but the defect/disorder in that act is reduced only to the free will, just as a limp is reduced to a crooked leg, not to the motive power itself
God directly wills and causes the defect in every sinful act
Sin has no relationship to being or act at all
P2Q79.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the act of sin considered as a being/action (traceable to God as First Cause of all actuality) from its defect or disorder, which is reduced to the free will falling away from God's order -- illustrated by the analogy of a limp being caused by a crooked leg, not by the power of movement itself.

P2Q79.q: According to Article 4, how does Aquinas explain that spiritual blindness can, in some cases, be directed toward the salvation of the one blinded?
options: Blindness never has any relation to salvation whatsoever
Though blindness of its nature tends toward damnation, God's mercy can direct temporary blindness medicinally, so that the predestined, recognizing their sin, are humbled and converted
Blindness is always a sign of certain damnation with no exceptions
Blindness only affects animals, not human souls
P2Q79.explanation: Aquinas explains that while blindness by its nature is ordered to the sinner's damnation, God's providence can direct it medicinally for the predestined, permitting a fall into sin so that, recognizing it, they may be humbled and converted, per Romans 8:28.

P2Q80.q: According to Article 1, why can the devil not be directly the cause of man's sin?
options: Because the devil has no power over human beings at all
Because sin's proper principle is the will, and nothing can be the direct cause of a sinful action except that which can move the will itself to act, which is not within the devil's power
Because sin is never actually caused by any external agent
Because the devil is himself incapable of understanding human choices
P2Q80.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since the proper principle of a sinful act is the will (every sin being voluntary), only something able to move the will itself could be a direct cause of sin -- and this the devil cannot do, since he cannot move the will directly.

P2Q80.q: According to Article 2, through which interior faculties does the devil operate to induce man to sin?
options: Directly through the intellect, by teaching false doctrines

Through the imagination and the sensitive appetite, by presenting certain forms to the imagination or inciting a passion, since he cannot directly move the will or enlighten the intellect toward truth
Directly through the will alone, bypassing all other faculties
Through no interior faculty; his influence is purely external and physical
P2Q80.explanation: Aquinas explains that since the devil has no intention of truly enlightening the intellect (his proper mode of moving it) and cannot move the will directly, his operation is confined to presenting images to the imagination or stirring passions in the sensitive appetite, thereby darkening reason indirectly.

P2Q80.q: According to Article 4, are all human sins directly the result of the devil's suggestion?
options: Yes, every single sin without exception is directly suggested by the devil

No -- the devil is only the occasional and indirect cause of all sin (through the corruption of nature from Adam's sin), not the direct cause of every individual sin, since natural desires like hunger could lead to sin even if the devil did not exist
Yes, because without the devil no human being would ever be tempted to sin
No, because the devil has no causal relationship whatsoever to human sin
P2Q80.explanation: Aquinas, citing Origen, argues the devil is only the indirect and occasional cause of sin generally (through the corruption of human nature stemming from Adam's sin), not the direct cause of every sin, since natural desires like food and sexual pleasure could become disordered even absent any demonic suggestion.

P2Q81.q: According to Article 1, what does Catholic faith require regarding the first sin of Adam and his descendants?
options: That each person's sin is entirely their own, with no inherited element from Adam at all, as the Pelagians held
That the first sin of the first man is transmitted to his descendants by way of origin, which is why infants are baptized soon after birth
That only the sins of one's immediate parents, not Adam's sin, are inherited
That original sin applies only to those who consciously choose to sin later in life
P2Q81.explanation: Aquinas states that Catholic faith requires holding that Adam's first sin is transmitted to his descendants by way of origin (hence infant baptism), against the Pelagian heresy which denied any such transmission.

P2Q81.q: According to Article 2, why are the other, later sins of Adam or of nearer ancestors NOT transmitted to their descendants, unlike the first sin?
options: Because only things pertaining to the nature of the species (not purely personal acts) are transmitted by generation, and personal actions like individual sinful choices are not part of what belongs to the species as such
Because God specifically forgives all sins committed after the first one
Because later sins are always less serious than the first sin
Because Adam stopped being capable of sinning after his first transgression
P2Q81.explanation: Aquinas argues that a father begets his child in species, not as an individual with identical personal history; only what pertains to human nature as such is transmitted (like having eyes), not purely personal acts -- illustrated by the fact a grammarian's son does not inherit his father's learned grammar.

P2Q81.q: According to Article 5, from which parent, according to Aquinas, would original sin be contracted, if only one of the two first parents had sinned?
options: Only from the mother, since she provides the matter for generation
Only from the father, since philosophers held that the active principle of generation comes from the father while the mother provides only the matter
From neither parent unless both had sinned together
Equally from either parent, regardless of which one sinned
P2Q81.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since original sin is transmitted through the active principle of generation, which philosophers attributed to the father (the mother providing only the matter), original sin would be contracted only if Adam, not Eve alone, had sinned.

P2Q82.q: According to Article 1, in what sense is original sin correctly called a 'habit'?
options: In the sense of a habit that inclines a power to act well, like science or virtue

In the sense of a disposition of a complex nature, whereby that nature is ill-disposed (like a second nature), comparable to bodily sickness, which is why original sin is called the 'languor of nature'
Original sin is not a habit in any sense whatsoever
In the sense of an action freely repeated many times by choice
P2Q82.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes habits that incline a power to act (like virtue) from habits as dispositions of a complex nature being well or ill disposed (like sickness); original sin is a habit only in the second sense, an inordinate disposition from the loss of original justice, called the 'languor of nature.'

P2Q82.q: According to Article 3, what is the 'formal' element of original sin, as opposed to its 'material' element?
options: Concupiscence is the formal element, while privation of original justice is merely material
The privation of original justice (the will's subjection to God) is the formal element, while the resulting disordered turning to mutable goods, called concupiscence, is the material element
Both concupiscence and the privation of original justice are equally and identically formal
Neither concupiscence nor privation of justice has any real role in original sin
P2Q82.explanation: Aquinas argues that since original justice consisted essentially in the will's subjection to God, the privation of that subjection is original sin's formal element, while the resulting general disorder of the soul's powers toward mutable goods, called concupiscence, is merely material.

P2Q82.q: According to Article 4, why is original sin equal in all who have it, rather than present in different degrees?
options: Because original sin, as the total privation of original justice, is like other total privations (such as death or darkness) which admit of no degrees, and all are equally related to the first principle (Adam's sin) from which it is transmitted
Because everyone commits exactly the same number of personal sins over a lifetime
Because original sin only affects the body, which is identical in every person
Because God arbitrarily assigns an equal degree of sin to every person
P2Q82.explanation: Aquinas reasons that original sin involves a total privation of original justice (like death or darkness, admitting no more or less), and that all descendants stand in an equal relation to Adam as the source of the corrupt origin, so original sin cannot be greater in one person than in another.

P2Q83.q: According to Article 1, in what sense is original sin 'in' the flesh, and in what sense is it properly 'in' the soul?
options: Original sin is in the flesh as its subject, and only accidentally in the soul
The flesh (bodily semen) is only the instrumental cause by which original sin is transmitted, but the soul alone is the proper subject in which original sin actually resides
Original sin resides equally and identically in both flesh and soul as co-subjects
Original sin has no relation to the body whatsoever, only to abstract guilt
P2Q83.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes being 'in' something as in a cause from being 'in' something as in a subject: Adam is the principal cause and the bodily semen the instrumental cause of transmission, but original sin can only actually reside, as its subject, in the soul.

P2Q83.q: According to Article 3, which power of the soul does original sin infect first, with respect to its inclination to act?
options: The intellect, since knowledge always precedes will in Aquinas's system
The will, since it is the power in which the first inclination to commit sin is seated
The imagination, since sin always begins with imagined images
The concupiscible power alone, to the exclusion of the will
P2Q83.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes original sin's inherence (which regards the soul's essence) from its inclination to act (which regards the powers); since the will is where the first inclination to sin is seated, original sin regards the will first among the powers.

P2Q83.q: According to Article 4, which three things does Aquinas single out as especially 'infected' by original sin, given how it is transmitted?
options: Only the intellect and memory, since original sin is primarily an intellectual defect
The generative power, and the delectation of touch belonging to the concupiscible faculty, because these are what concur in the act of generation by which original sin is transmitted
Only the powers involved in speech and communication
The powers of sight and hearing exclusively
P2Q83.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since original sin is transmitted through the act of generation, the powers that concur in that act -- the generative power and the concupiscible faculty's delectation of touch -- are said to be especially corrupted and infected, though all the soul's parts are affected in some way.

P2Q84.q: According to Article 1, in what sense can covetousness be called the 'root' of all sins?
options: Only in the sense of inordinate desire specifically for riches

In the sense of an inclination of corrupt nature to desire corruptible goods inordinately, comparable to a root drawing sustenance from earth, since every sin grows out of some love of temporal things
Covetousness cannot be called the root of sin in any sense, according to Aquinas
Only because covetousness is explicitly listed first among the Ten Commandments
P2Q84.explanation: Aquinas explains that covetousness, understood as the corrupt nature's inclination to desire corruptible goods inordinately, is called the 'root' of sin because, like a root drawing nourishment from the earth, every sin in some way grows out of an inordinate love of temporal things.

P2Q84.q: According to Article 2, how does pride, as the 'beginning' of every sin, differ from covetousness as the 'root' of every sin?
options: They are entirely identical concepts with no real distinction

Covetousness regards sin's turning toward the mutable good that nourishes it (hence 'root'), while pride regards sin's turning away from God's commandment, refusing subjection to Him (hence 'beginning,' since turning away from God begins evil)
Pride only concerns physical vanity, unrelated to spiritual matters
Covetousness is worse than pride in every case, according to Aquinas
P2Q84.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the two: covetousness names sin's turning toward the mutable good that nourishes and fosters it (hence a 'root'), while pride names sin's turning away from God's rule and refusal of subjection to Him, which is why it is called the 'beginning' of evil.

P2Q84.q: According to Article 3, what makes a vice 'capital' in Aquinas's technical sense, as opposed to merely a sin punishable by death?
options: A capital vice is simply any sin serious enough to warrant execution under civil law

A capital vice is one from which other vices arise, chiefly by being their final cause -- it functions as a principle and 'director' of other vices, much like a head directs the body or a leader directs an army
A capital vice is any vice condemned specifically in the Ten Commandments
A capital vice is one committed only by people in positions of authority
P2Q84.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that in this context 'capital' is a metaphor from 'head' as principle/director rather than referring to capital punishment: a capital vice gives rise to and directs other vices chiefly as their final cause, like the leaders of an army, per Gregory's comparison.

P2Q85.q: According to Article 1, what threefold good of human nature does Aquinas distinguish when discussing how sin affects it?
options: Wealth, health, and reputation
The constitutive principles of nature (like the soul's powers), the natural inclination to virtue, and the gift of original justice
Faith, hope, and charity
Strength, beauty, and intelligence
P2Q85.explanation: Aquinas identifies three goods of human nature: the natural constitutive principles (powers of the soul), the natural inclination to virtue that flows from being rational, and the gift of original justice originally conferred on human nature as a whole.

P2Q85.q: According to Article 2, why can sin never entirely destroy the good of human nature (the natural inclination to virtue)?
options: Because sin actually strengthens the natural inclination to virtue over time
Because this inclination follows from man simply being a rational being, and sin cannot remove man's rationality entirely -- if it did, he would no longer be capable of sin at all
Because God directly prevents any sin from having lasting effects on nature
Because the inclination to virtue is located in the body, not the soul, and thus cannot be affected by sin
P2Q85.explanation: Aquinas argues that the natural inclination to virtue belongs to man simply because he is rational, and since sin cannot remove man's rational nature (or he could no longer sin at all, sin itself requiring rational capacity), this good of nature can be diminished but never wholly destroyed.

P2Q85.q: According to Article 5, in what way are death and other bodily defects effects of sin, according to Aquinas?
options: Directly and essentially, since the sinner always positively intends to bring about death

Accidentally, in the sense that Adam's sin removed the gift of original justice which had held the body in perfect subjection to the soul, thereby removing an obstacle to bodily corruption, rather than directly causing it
Death and bodily defects have no relation whatsoever to sin
Only the personal sins of each individual cause that individual's own death, with no connection to Adam
P2Q85.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes a cause acting by reason of itself (producing an intended effect) from an accidental cause (which acts by removing an obstacle); since death is beside the sinner's intention, Adam's sin caused it accidentally, by removing the gift of original justice that had preserved the body from corruption.

P2Q86.q: According to Article 1, what does the 'stain' on the soul caused by sin metaphorically represent?
options: A literal physical mark visible on the sinner's body

The loss of the soul's comeliness -- from the light of natural reason and from the light of Divine wisdom and grace -- that occurs when the soul cleaves inordinately, through love, to things contrary to that light
A permanent, unforgivable curse placed on the sinner by God
A social label imposed by the community upon a known sinner
P2Q86.explanation: Aquinas explains that just as a comely body loses its beauty through contact with something soiling, the soul, which has a comeliness from reason's natural light and from Divine wisdom and grace, loses that comeliness -- called a 'stain' -- when it cleaves through love to things against that light.

P2Q86.q: According to Article 2, why does the stain of sin remain in the soul even after the sinful act itself has ended?
options: Because the stain is actually permanent and can never be removed by any means

Because merely ceasing the act does not restore the soul to its previous nearness to the light of reason and Divine law; a contrary movement of the will (a return via grace) is needed, just as parted persons need a movement toward each other to be reunited
Because God chooses at random which sinners remain stained
Because the stain is unrelated to the act of sin and instead depends only on external punishment
P2Q86.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of two people separated by a movement: ceasing the movement does not reunite them, they must move back toward each other; likewise the soul remains withdrawn from the light of reason and Divine law until a contrary movement, aided by grace, brings it back.

P2Q87.q: According to Article 4, what are the two components of punishment corresponding to the two elements Aquinas identifies within sin itself?
options: Physical pain and mental anguish, corresponding to bodily and spiritual sins respectively

The 'pain of loss,' corresponding to sin's turning away from the infinite immutable good (and so itself infinite), and the 'pain of sense,' corresponding to sin's inordinate turning toward a finite mutable good (and so itself finite)
Excommunication and civil punishment, corresponding to spiritual and temporal sins
There is only one undifferentiated form of punishment for every sin
P2Q87.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes sin's turning away from the infinite immutable good (God), whose corresponding punishment is the infinite 'pain of loss,' from sin's inordinate turning toward a finite mutable good, whose corresponding punishment is the finite 'pain of sense.'

P2Q87.q: According to Article 3, why does a sin that destroys charity (turning man away from God as his last end) incur a debt of eternal punishment?
options: Because all sins, without exception, incur eternal punishment equally

Because such sin destroys the very principle of the order by which man's will is subject to God (the last end, held by charity), and a defect that destroys a principle is, of itself, irreparable by natural means, unlike defects that leave the principle intact
Because eternal punishment is simply an arbitrary decree with no explanatory rationale
Because such sins are always publicly known and therefore must be publicly and permanently punished
P2Q87.explanation: Aquinas reasons that when a sin destroys the principle of the order of Divine justice -- the last end held onto by charity -- the resulting disorder is, considered in itself, irreparable (unlike defects that leave the underlying principle intact and so can be remedied), which is why such sin incurs a debt of eternal punishment.

P2Q87.q: According to Article 6, why does the debt of punishment remain even after the sinful act itself has ceased?
options: Because punishment is entirely unrelated to any act of sin

Because the act of sin makes a person deserving of punishment as a matter of Divine justice, and restoring the 'equality of justice' requires a penal compensation, which does not occur automatically just because the act has stopped
Because God punishes people randomly regardless of whether they sinned
Because the debt of punishment only ever applies to sins committed against other people, not against God
P2Q87.explanation: Aquinas argues that transgressing the order of Divine justice makes one deserving of punishment, and this debt persists until repaid by some penal compensation restoring the equality of justice -- so the debt outlasts the sinful act itself, just as debts owed for injuries to others persist after the injurious act ends.

P2Q88.q: According to Article 2, what makes a sin 'venial' rather than mortal 'from the cause' or 'totally'?
options: A venial sin is one the sinner never regrets committing

A sin may be venial because something diminishes its guilt (like weakness or ignorance), or because it does not destroy the order to the last end and so deserves only temporal, not eternal, punishment
A venial sin is any sin that is never discovered by other people
A sin is venial only if it is committed against oneself rather than against another person
P2Q88.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes sin venial 'from the cause' (something like weakness or ignorance partially diminishes guilt) from sin venial 'totally' (it does not destroy the order to the last end and so merits only temporal punishment), and it is this latter sense he focuses on.

P2Q88.q: According to Article 3, in what way can repeated venial sins disposes a person toward committing mortal sin?
options: Venial sin has no relationship whatsoever to the possibility of mortal sin

Either directly, by strengthening a habit until the sinner fixes his end in that venial sin, or indirectly, by habituating the will not to be subject to due order in lesser matters, disposing it to also disregard the order to the last end
Only by literally being the same act repeated with a change of intention
By automatically converting into mortal sin after a fixed number of repetitions
P2Q88.explanation: Aquinas explains two ways: directly, when repeated venial acts strengthen a habit so strongly that the sinner comes to fix his end in it; and indirectly, when habituating the will to disregard due order in small matters disposes it to eventually disregard the order to the last end itself, which is mortal sin.

P2Q88.q: According to Article 6, why can a mortal sin never become a venial sin by some addition, even though a venial sin can become mortal?
options: Because mortal and venial sins are not actually different from one another in any way

Because venial and mortal differ as imperfect and perfect in the genus of sin -- the imperfect can be perfected by addition, but the perfect cannot be reduced to imperfect merely by an addition; an added deformity only aggravates an already mortal sin further
Because mortal sins can always be forgiven, unlike venial sins
Because Aquinas holds there is actually no difference in severity between the two
P2Q88.explanation: Aquinas reasons that venial and mortal sin stand as imperfect to perfect within the genus of sin; the imperfect can be completed by an addition (venial becoming mortal, e.g., an idle word spoken for the sake of fornication), but adding to something already perfect (mortal) cannot make it imperfect -- it can only aggravate it further.

P2Q89.q: According to Article 4, why can neither good nor wicked angels sin venially?
options: Because angels cannot sin at all, whether mortally or venially

Because an angel's non-discursive intellect considers the means only under the order to the end it has already fixed on, so any disorder regarding the means implies disorder regarding the end itself, which is mortal sin -- good angels' ends are always ordered to God, wicked angels' always to their sin of pride
Because venial sin requires a physical body, which angels lack
Because angels are incapable of choosing between alternatives of any kind
P2Q89.explanation: Aquinas argues that because angelic intellects do not reason discursively from principles to conclusions the way humans do, an angel's consideration of means (like conclusions) cannot be disordered unless the end (like a principle) is also disordered -- and disorder regarding the end is mortal sin, so no venial sin is possible for angels of either kind.

P2Q89.q: According to Article 6, why can venial sin never exist in a person together with original sin alone, without any mortal sin?
options: Because original sin automatically becomes venial sin once a person is baptized

Because before the age of reason a person is incapable of any personal sin (venial or mortal), and once reason is attained, the very first act of moral deliberation either directs the person to God (removing original sin by grace) or, if not, constitutes a mortal sin -- leaving no room for venial sin alone with unremoved original sin
Because venial sin is impossible for anyone who has ever been baptized as an infant
Because original sin and venial sin are actually the same thing under different names
P2Q89.explanation: Aquinas reasons that before the use of reason a child cannot sin at all, and at the very moment reason first functions, the person's foundational choice either turns them to their due end (receiving grace that removes original sin) or fails to do so, which itself constitutes a mortal sin -- so there is no interval where venial sin alone could coexist with unremoved original sin.

P2Q89.q: According to Article 5, why are the mere first movements of the sensitive appetite in unbelievers, prior to full consent, not mortal sins?
options: Because unbelievers are incapable of sinning mortally under any circumstances

Because the sensuality itself cannot be the subject of mortal sin (as established earlier), and this holds regardless of whether the person is a believer or unbeliever, since the excellence or lack of excellence in a person's state never diminishes the gravity of a sin but can only increase it
Because unbelievers do not actually have a sensitive appetite
Because only believers can commit venial sins, while unbelievers can only commit mortal sins
P2Q89.explanation: Aquinas gives two reasons: sensuality itself cannot be the subject of mortal sin in anyone, believer or not, and since the excellence of one's state (like being a believer, with greater knowledge and grace) only ever aggravates a sin rather than diminishing it, mere unconsented movements are no more mortal in unbelievers than in believers.

P2Q90.q: According to Article 1, why does Aquinas conclude that law pertains to reason rather than, say, to the will alone?
options: Because law is derived from 'ligare,' meaning to bind, with no connection to reason at all

Because the rule and measure of human acts is reason, which directs acts to their end, and just as the principle in any genus serves as its rule and measure, reason is the rule and measure that gives law its character
Because only emotions, not reason, can effectively compel human behavior
Because Aquinas holds that reason and law are simply identical terms with no distinction
P2Q90.explanation: Aquinas argues that since reason is the first principle directing human acts to their end, and the principle of any genus serves as its rule and measure, and since law is precisely a rule and measure of acts, law must belong to reason.

P2Q90.q: According to Article 2, to what must law be principally directed, according to Aquinas?
options: The private benefit of the lawgiver alone

The common good, since law regards the first principle of practical reason (the last end, happiness), and since individuals are parts of the community, law must regard the happiness of the whole community
The preservation of ancient customs regardless of their current usefulness
The personal advancement of whichever individual enforces the law
P2Q90.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since law is referred to the chief principle in practical matters (the last end, happiness), and since each person is part of the larger community, law must be principally concerned with the common good, that is, the happiness of the whole community, not merely private benefit.

P2Q90.q: According to Article 4, why is promulgation essential for something to have the binding force of law?
options: Promulgation is merely a formality with no real bearing on a law's binding force
A rule or measure only takes effect by being applied to those it is meant to regulate, and this application happens through the law being made known to them by promulgation
Promulgation is required only for laws concerning taxation, not other matters
Laws bind automatically upon being written down, whether or not anyone else learns of them
P2Q90.explanation: Aquinas argues that since a law is imposed as a rule and measure upon those who are to be ruled by it, it must actually be applied to them, and this application occurs through promulgation -- without which the law cannot obtain the binding force proper to law.

P2Q91.q: According to Article 1, what is the eternal law, as Aquinas defines it?
options: A set of civil statutes that never expire
The type (or plan) of Divine Wisdom, as it directs all the actions and movements of the universe toward their due end, existing timelessly in God the Ruler of all things
A law that applies only to angels, not to any material creature
A synonym for the Ten Commandments given at Sinai
P2Q91.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as an artificer has a type or plan of what he will make, so God as Ruler of the universe has, in His Wisdom, the type of the order of all things He directs to their end; since this Divine conception is not subject to time, it is called the eternal law.

P2Q91.q: According to Article 2, what is the natural law, according to Aquinas's definition?
options: A set of laws enacted by human legislatures based on natural resources
The rational creature's participation in the eternal law, whereby it has a natural inclination to its proper act and end, in a manner higher than that of non-rational creatures
A law that applies exclusively to non-human animals
An arbitrary set of customs that vary completely from culture to culture with no common basis
P2Q91.explanation: Aquinas explains that while all creatures are ruled by the eternal law and derive their inclinations from it, the rational creature partakes of it in a more excellent way, being provident for itself and others; this participation of the eternal law in the rational creature is called the natural law.

P2Q91.q: According to Article 4, why was a Divine law necessary in addition to natural and human law?
options: Because natural and human law are entirely useless and should be abolished

Because man is ordained to an end of eternal happiness that surpasses what is proportionate to his natural faculties, so a further direction from God, beyond what natural and human law (derived from it) can provide, was necessary
Because human law was thought to be too harsh without Divine law to soften it
Because Divine law was needed only to regulate the behavior of civil rulers
