P2Q91.explanation: Aquinas argues that since man's natural and human law suffice to direct him toward ends proportionate to his natural capacity, but man is also ordained toward a supernatural end of eternal happiness disproportionate to his natural powers, a further Divine law was necessary to direct him toward that higher end.

P2Q92.q: According to Article 1, what is the proper effect of law, according to Aquinas?
options: To enrich the lawgiver at the expense of the subjects

To lead its subjects to their proper virtue, and thus make them good -- simply good, if the lawgiver's intention is fixed on the true common good, or good only in a qualified respect, if aimed at something merely useful or pleasurable to the lawgiver
To have no effect whatsoever on the moral character of those who obey it
To punish wrongdoers exclusively, with no positive formative effect on anyone
P2Q92.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the virtue of any subordinate thing lies in being well subjected to what regulates it, and law aims at obedience, the proper effect of law is to lead its subjects to virtue and thus make them good -- simply good if the lawgiver aims at the true common good, or good only relative to a particular regime otherwise.

P2Q92.q: According to Article 1, how does Aquinas explain the paradoxical phrase 'a good robber'?
options: It shows that Aquinas believes theft can sometimes be virtuous in itself

Good can be found even in things bad in themselves when something works in a way well-adapted to its (flawed) end, illustrating how a law oriented to something other than the true common good makes people good only in a qualified, relative sense
It is a printing error and does not appear in Aquinas's actual argument
It refers only to robbers who later repent and join a monastery
P2Q92.explanation: Aquinas uses this phrase to illustrate that 'good' can apply even to something bad in itself when it operates well relative to its own (flawed) end, paralleling how a law not aimed at the true common good can still make its subjects 'good' only in a qualified sense relative to that particular regime.

P2Q92.q: According to Article 2, what analogy does Aquinas draw between law and reasoning in the demonstrative sciences?
options: Law has nothing whatsoever in common with reasoning of any kind
Just as reason in demonstrative sciences leads from principles to assent to a conclusion, law as a dictate of reason similarly induces people, by some means, to assent to and obey its precept
Law is compared to poetry rather than to any form of reasoning
The analogy is between law and mere guesswork, since law has no rational structure
P2Q92.explanation: Aquinas observes that just as an assertion is reason's dictate asserting something, law is reason's dictate commanding something; and just as demonstrative reasoning leads from principles to a conclusion, law similarly leads its subjects, by some rational means, to assent to what it commands.

P2Q93.q: According to Article 1, what is the eternal law identical with, according to Aquinas?
options: A body of civil statutes enacted by earthly rulers
The very type of Divine Wisdom, insofar as it directs all actions and movements of creatures to their due end, just as an artificer's plan directs the products of his art
A collection of miracles recorded in Scripture
The moral conscience of every individual human being
P2Q93.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as an artificer's plan (his art or exemplar) directs the products he makes, so God's Wisdom, as it moves all creatures to their due end, has the character of a law -- and this is precisely what the eternal law is.

P2Q93.q: According to Article 2, in what sense is the eternal law 'known to all,' according to Aquinas?
options: All people, even the wicked, see the eternal law directly and completely in its very essence

No one can know the eternal law as it is in itself except the blessed who see God's Essence, but every rational creature knows it to some degree in its reflection or effects, at least through common principles of the natural law
Only professional theologians can have any knowledge of the eternal law
The eternal law cannot be known by anyone at all, even partially, in this life
P2Q93.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes knowing a thing in itself from knowing it through its effects (like knowing the sun through its rays); only the blessed see the eternal law in itself, but every rational creature has some reflected knowledge of it, at least regarding the common principles of the natural law.

P2Q93.q: According to Article 4, which things are NOT subject to the eternal law, according to Aquinas?
options: Nothing whatsoever is exempt from the eternal law, including God's own nature

Things pertaining to the Divine Nature or Essence itself are not subject to the eternal law but are rather identical with the eternal law itself, whereas everything else, whether contingent or necessary, created by God is subject to it
Only inanimate objects like rocks and rivers are exempt from the eternal law
Human beings alone are exempt from the eternal law, though animals remain subject to it
P2Q93.explanation: Aquinas draws an analogy to human government (where what pertains to human nature itself, like having a soul, is not subject to human law) to argue that everything created, contingent or necessary, is subject to the eternal law, while what pertains to the Divine Nature or Essence simply is the eternal law, not subject to it.

P2Q94.q: According to Article 3, do all specific virtuous acts, considered in their proper species, belong to the natural law?
options: Yes, every specific virtuous act in every detail is directly prescribed by the natural law with no need for reasoning

Considered simply as virtuous (i.e., as in accord with reason), all virtuous acts belong to the natural law since reason naturally inclines man to act virtuously; but considered in their proper specific details, not all virtuous acts are prescribed by nature, since many were discovered by reason's inquiry as conducive to good living
No virtuous acts whatsoever belong to the natural law
Only acts of the cardinal virtues, and none of the theological virtues, belong to natural law
P2Q94.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes virtuous acts considered simply as virtuous (belonging to natural law, since man's rational nature inclines him to act according to reason) from virtuous acts considered in their specific detailed forms (not all of which are natural, many being discovered through reason's inquiry as useful for good living).

P2Q94.q: According to Article 4, is the natural law exactly the same in all men, in every detail?
options: Yes, completely identical in every particular application without exception, just like in speculative sciences

The general principles of the natural law are the same for all, but as one descends to particular matters of action (which involve contingent circumstances), the practical rectitude derived from those principles is not equally the same, nor equally known, to everyone
No, the natural law varies completely and arbitrarily from person to person with no shared principles at all
The natural law applies only to speculative, not practical, matters, so the question does not arise
P2Q94.explanation: Aquinas contrasts speculative reason (dealing with necessary things, where truth is the same for all both in principles and conclusions) with practical reason (dealing with contingent human actions), concluding that natural law's general principles are shared by all, but detailed conclusions can vary and are not equally known to everyone.

P2Q94.q: According to Article 6, can the natural law be entirely blotted out from the human heart?
options: Yes, both the most general and the more detailed precepts of natural law can be completely and permanently erased from everyone without exception

The most general precepts cannot be blotted out in the abstract (though application in a particular case can be blocked by passion), but the secondary, more detailed precepts can be blotted out from the heart through evil persuasion or vicious customs and corrupt habits
No part of the natural law can ever be blotted out under any circumstances, even in a particular action
The natural law can be blotted out only by direct Divine intervention, never by human vice
P2Q94.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the most general precepts of natural law, which cannot be abstractly erased from the human heart (though their application can be blocked in a particular act by passion), from secondary precepts, which can indeed be blotted out by evil persuasion or entrenched vicious customs, as with certain peoples who did not regard theft or unnatural vices as sinful.

P2Q95.q: According to Article 1, why does Aquinas argue it was useful for human laws to be framed?
options: Because human laws are the only means by which anyone can ever become virtuous

Because while paternal admonition suffices for those well-disposed to virtue by nature or good upbringing, others who are prone to vice and not easily persuaded by words need to be restrained from evil by the force and fear that only law provides, eventually habituating them to virtue
Because laws exist purely to punish, with no role in forming virtuous character at all
Because animals also require laws in order to behave properly
P2Q95.explanation: Aquinas argues that while some people, well-disposed by nature or upbringing, can be guided toward virtue through paternal admonition alone, those inclined to vice and resistant to persuasion need to be restrained by the fear of legal punishment, which habituates them over time to willingly do what they once did only from fear.

P2Q95.q: According to Article 2, what happens to a human law that deviates from the natural law?
options: It remains fully valid law regardless of any deviation from natural law
It has just so much of the nature of law as it derives from the natural law; insofar as it deflects from natural law in any point, it is no longer a law but a corruption or perversion of law
It automatically becomes Divine law instead of human law
Such deviation is impossible, since human law and natural law can never conflict
P2Q95.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the force of law depends on its justice, which is measured against the rule of reason (whose first rule is the natural law), a human law that deviates from the natural law loses its character as true law and becomes merely a corruption of law.

P2Q95.q: According to Article 4, how does Aquinas distinguish the 'law of nations' from 'civil law' within human positive law?
options: The law of nations concerns only international treaties, while civil law concerns only domestic matters

The law of nations comprises things derived from natural law as conclusions from premises (like just buying and selling, necessary for social life), while civil law comprises things derived from natural law by particular determination, as each state decides what is best for itself
There is no real distinction; the two terms are simply synonyms in Aquinas's usage
The law of nations applies to Christians only, while civil law applies to non-Christians
P2Q95.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes two ways things can be derived from natural law: as conclusions follow from premises (giving rise to the law of nations, e.g., rules of just exchange necessary for social life) and by particular determination suited to each community (giving rise to civil law, which varies by what each state judges best).

P2Q96.q: According to Article 2, why does Aquinas hold that human law should NOT attempt to repress every vice?
options: Because vice is not actually harmful to society, so there is no need to repress it

Because a law, as a measure, must be proportioned to the condition of those it measures -- what is possible for a person lacking a virtuous habit differs from what is possible for the virtuous, so human law must be framed as something possible according to the customs and capacities of ordinary people, not the perfectly virtuous alone
Because repressing vice is solely the responsibility of the Church, never of civil law
Because Aquinas believes vice should instead be encouraged by human law for practical reasons
P2Q96.explanation: Aquinas argues that law, like any measure, must be proportioned to what it measures; since not everyone has attained virtuous habits, human law must be framed as something possible for people generally (as Isidore says, 'possible according to nature and custom'), tolerating certain things in the imperfect that would be blameworthy in the virtuous.

P2Q96.q: According to Article 4, under what conditions does a human law bind in conscience, according to Aquinas?
options: Human law never binds in conscience, only in the external legal forum

When the law is just -- ordained to the common good, made within the lawgiver's authority, and imposing burdens proportionately -- it binds in conscience because it derives that binding force from the eternal law itself
Only laws that impose the death penalty bind in conscience
Any law whatsoever binds in conscience automatically regardless of its content
P2Q96.explanation: Aquinas argues that just laws -- just from their end (ordained to the common good), their author (within the lawgiver's proper authority), and their form (proportionate burdens) -- bind in conscience because their power to bind derives ultimately from the eternal law, while unjust laws lack this same binding force in conscience.

P2Q96.q: According to Article 6, when may someone justly act against the letter of a law, according to Aquinas's besieged-city example?
options: Never; the literal text of a law must always be followed no matter the consequences

When following the letter of the law in a particular unforeseen case would actually work against the very common good the lawgiver intended to promote by that law -- as when the rule to keep city gates shut would, in one case, doom the city's own defenders fleeing the enemy
Only when a judge personally dislikes the law in question
Only in matters of religious law, never in matters of civil law
P2Q96.explanation: Aquinas argues that since law is shaped for what happens in the majority of cases and aimed at the common good, a case where literal observance would harm the common good the lawgiver intended (like refusing to open a besieged city's gates to its fleeing defenders) justifies acting against the letter of the law.

P2Q97.q: According to Article 1, what is one legitimate cause, on the part of reason itself, for changing human law over time?
options: Laws should never be changed once enacted, regardless of circumstances

Human reason naturally advances gradually from the imperfect to the more perfect, so early lawgivers, unable to consider everything, set up institutions later found deficient, which subsequent lawgivers justly improved upon
Laws should be changed as often as possible purely to keep citizens uncertain
Only religious authorities, never civil lawgivers, are permitted to alter any law
P2Q97.explanation: Aquinas compares practical to speculative reasoning: just as early philosophers' teaching was later perfected by successors, early lawgivers' institutions, being imperfect and deficient in various ways, were justly improved by later lawgivers seeking to better serve the common good.

P2Q97.q: According to Article 2, why does Aquinas argue that human law should NOT be changed every time something better occurs to someone?
options: Because change is impossible once a law has been promulgated

Because the very act of changing a law is, to some extent, prejudicial to the common good since custom greatly aids the observance of laws, so change should occur only when compensated by a very evident benefit or an urgent necessity
Because only kings, and no other lawgivers, have the authority to change laws
Because Aquinas believed no law could ever actually be improved upon
P2Q97.explanation: Aquinas reasons that changing a law diminishes its binding power insofar as it undermines the custom that aids legal observance, so law should be changed only when the change is justified by a clearly great benefit or by the urgent harm of an unjust or gravely harmful existing law.

P2Q97.q: According to Article 3, how can custom obtain the force of law, according to Aquinas?
options: Custom can never have any legal force whatsoever, only written statutes count

Because law proceeds from the reason and will of the lawgiver, which can be manifested not only by speech but also by repeated deeds, which most effectively declare the deliberate judgment of reason and will, since 'when a thing is done again and again, it seems to proceed from a deliberate judgment of reason'
Custom obtains force of law automatically the very first time an act is performed, with no repetition needed
Custom can only ever abolish law, never establish new legal obligations
P2Q97.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as human speech manifests the interior reason and will that make law, repeated actions can likewise manifest that same reason and will even more effectively, since repeated conduct signals a deliberate judgment -- so custom can establish, expound, or abolish law.
